text:
So let us step back and look at the big picture. These ten frameworks are not competitors. They are complements. Each one attacks your causal claim from a different angle.

E values and Rosenbaum Bounds quantify how strong unmeasured confounding would need to be. Negative Controls and Placebo Tests detect when something is wrong with your study design. Instrumental Variables and Regression Discontinuity provide alternative identification strategies that sidestep confounding entirely, at least locally. Difference in Differences exploits temporal variation. Manski Bounds give you honest intervals under minimal assumptions. Falsification Tests stress test your specific causal model. And DAG based Sensitivity Analysis lets you reason transparently about what you might be missing.

The comparison matrix breaks down like this. For unmeasured confounding, almost all ten frameworks help in some way. For selection bias, IV, RD, Manski Bounds, and Falsification Tests are your best tools. For reverse causation, IV, RD, and DiD help because they use temporal or structural separation. For model misspecification, Negative Controls, Placebo Tests, Manski Bounds, and Falsification Tests are the detectors.

The takeaway is simple. Never rely on one framework. Stack them. If your causal claim survives E values, passes placebo tests, holds up under Rosenbaum bounds, and makes correct falsification predictions, you are in strong shape. Not certain, never certain, but strong. And if it fails even one of these tests, that is not a disaster. That is information. It tells you exactly where your claim is vulnerable and what you need to investigate next. That is what causal robustness is all about. Not proving you are right, but systematically trying to prove you are wrong, and failing.
